analysis.one_liner: Requires lenders to report applicant race, sex, and age data so regulators can catch lending discrimination.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2019 and never received a hearing or a vote; it died in committee at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Equal Credit Opportunity Act to require lenders to collect demographic information from people applying for certain kinds of credit, including car loans, credit cards, payday loans, and loans with interest rates above 36 percent. Lenders would report that data, along with approval or rejection decisions and reasons, to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau each year. The agency would use the data to spot lenders that discriminate by race, sex, age, marital status, sexual orientation, or gender identity, and could fine violators or refer cases to the Justice Department.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers applying for car loans, credit cards, and small or high-interest loans, especially members of groups that have historically faced discrimination in lending. The bill would give regulators and the public the data needed to identify lenders that approve or reject applicants based on race, sex, age, marital status, sexual orientation, or gender identity, and it would require the Bureau to post approval and rejection patterns online for anyone to inspect.

how_it_helps.text: Requires creditors in car loans, credit cards, payday loans, and loans above 36 percent APR or under $15,000 to collect applicant demographic data and report approval or rejection decisions, reasons, credit scores, and debt-to-income ratios to the CFPB annually [S3].
Directs the Bureau to use that data to determine whether a creditor discriminates and to take enforcement action, including civil penalties and referrals to the Attorney General [S2].
The Bureau must post the aggregated data online in a form the public can access without special software, and bar creditors from sharing or using applicant demographic data for marketing [S3].
Applicants may refuse to provide the demographic information, and underwriters may not access it while deciding applications, so the data cannot be used to discriminate during underwriting [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Lenders that make car loans, credit cards, small-dollar loans, and high-interest loans would bear the cost of collecting, protecting, and annually reporting application data, and would face new exposure to enforcement and civil penalties if the data shows discriminatory patterns. Applicants would spend a little extra time answering optional demographic questions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Auto, credit card, and payday lenders

drawbacks.text: The reporting mandate applies to a wide slice of the lending market, including ordinary car and credit card loans, so compliance costs would fall on many mainstream lenders and could be passed along to borrowers in the form of higher fees [S3].

Collecting race, sexual orientation, and gender identity data from loan applicants raises privacy concerns, and while the bill bars underwriters from accessing the data and allows refusal, a creditor that determines underwriters should have access may proceed after notifying the applicant [S3].
The bill includes safe harbors for unintentional reporting errors, which could limit how strictly the new data requirements are enforced against creditors [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill creates a real transparency tool: lending discrimination is hard to prove without data, and the bill would give regulators and the public the numbers they currently lack. The costs are real but routine for a data-reporting regime, and the bill includes privacy protections and error safe harbors that soften the burden on lenders. The main weakness is not design but fate: it drew no cosponsors and never advanced, so the benefits and costs never materialized.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died at the end of the 116th Congress without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jesus G. "Chuy" Garcia, a Democrat from Illinois, introduced the bill on April 15, 2019 [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lenders that make car loans, credit cards, and small or high-interest loans avoided a new annual data-reporting obligation and the enforcement exposure that would have come with it. Borrowers who experience lending discrimination gained nothing, since the data that would reveal discriminatory patterns is still not collected.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Auto, credit card, and payday lenders

for.name: Rep. Jesus G. "Chuy" Garcia
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor [S1].

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsor signed on, so the partisan shape of the fight was never visible; the bill simply stalled in committee with a single Democratic sponsor.

industries.industry: Consumer lenders (auto finance, credit card issuers, payday and high-rate installment lenders)
industries.note: These lenders would have had to collect demographic data from applicants, file annual reports with the CFPB, and open themselves to enforcement if the data showed discriminatory approval patterns. Their interest in avoiding reporting and enforcement ran against borrowers' interest in having discrimination documented.
Loans above 36 percent APR and loans under $15,000 or under three years were squarely covered, so payday and subprime lenders would have faced the closest scrutiny under the new data regime.
